claim: The synaptonemal complex (SC) is an evolutionarily-conserved protein assembly that holds together homologous chromosomes during prophase of the first meiotic division.
source: The synaptonemal complex (SC) is an evolutionarily-conserved protein assembly that holds together homologous chromosomes during prophase of the first meiotic division.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about the SC supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Human SYCP3 forms a highly-elongated helical tetramer of 20 nm length.
source: Here we show that human SYCP3 forms a highly-elongated helical tetramer of 20 nm length.
evidence: Supported by SEC-MALS data showing tetrameric molecular weight and crystal structure showing 20 nm length.

claim: N-terminal sequences extending from each end of the SYCP3 rod-like structure bind double-stranded DNA.
source: N-terminal sequences extending from each end of the rod-like structure bind double-stranded DNA, enabling SYCP3 to link distant sites along the sister chromatid.
evidence: Supported by EMSA and fluorescence anisotropy experiments showing DNA binding dependent on N-terminal basic patches.

claim: SYCP3 self-assembles into regular filamentous structures that resemble the known morphology of the SC lateral element.
source: We further find that SYCP3 self-assembles into regular filamentous structures that resemble the known morphology of the SC lateral element.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy showing striated fibres with 23 nm periodicity.

claim: Disruption of SC formation in mice leads to meiotic failure, infertility and embryonic death through aneuploidy.
source: disruption of SC formation in mice leads to meiotic failure, infertility and embryonic death through aneuploidy (Yuan et al., 2000, 2002; de Vries et al., 2005; Kouznetsova et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Defective SC formation in humans has been associated with cases of infertility and recurrent miscarriage.
source: Defective SC formation in humans has been associated with cases of infertility and recurrent miscarriage, which overall affect 15% and 5% of couples respectively, in addition to non-lethal aneuploidies such as Down's syndrome (Matzuk and Lamb, 2002; Sierra and Stephenson, 2006; Bolor et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: The SC adopts the same characteristic tripartite structure in all sexually reproducing organisms in which it is found, from yeast to humans.
source: These studies have shown that the SC adopts the same characteristic tripartite structure in all sexually reproducing organisms in which it is found, from yeast to humans (Figure 1A; Moses, 1968; Westergaard and von Wettstein, 1972).
evidence: Supported by citations to electron microscopy studies and Figure 1A showing the structure.

claim: The SC is comprised of two approximately 50 nm wide lateral elements (LEs) and a 100 nm wide central region.
source: Thus, the SC is comprised of two approximately 50 nm wide lateral elements (LEs) that coat the chromosome axes, and a 100 nm wide central region that in almost all organisms contains a mid-line 20–40 nm wide central element (CE).
evidence: Based on established ultrastructural knowledge from electron microscopy studies.

claim: SYCP2 and SYCP3 are the main constituents of the lateral element.
source: According to this initial map of the SC, the SYCE1, SYCE2, SYCE3 and TEX12 proteins form the central element, whilst SYCP2 and SYCP3 are the main constituents of the lateral element (Figure 1B; Costa et al., 2005; Hamer et al., 2006; Schramm et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to immunofluorescence and immunogold staining studies and Figure 1B.

claim: SYCP1 forms the transverse filaments with its N- and C-termini located in the central and lateral elements respectively.
source: The transverse filaments are formed by SYCP1, with its N- and C-termini located in the central and lateral elements respectively (Liu et al., 1996; Schmekel et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Disruption of SYCP3 in mice leads to complete infertility in males owing to apoptotic cell death during meiotic prophase.
source: In males, it causes complete infertility owing to apoptotic cell death during meiotic prophase, with failure of SC formation and synapsis (Yuan et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to published mouse study.

claim: SYCP3 deficiency in female mice causes subfertility with a high aneuploidy rate leading to embryonic death in utero.
source: in females, there is subfertility, with a high aneuploidy rate leading to embryonic death in utero (Yuan et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published mouse study.

claim: SYCP3 deficiency causes a doubling of chromosome axis length with respect to wild type.
source: SYCP3 deficiency has two intriguing structural consequences for the chromosome axis: a doubling of chromosome axis length with respect to wild type, and premature disassembly of the cohesin cores during diplotene (Yuan et al., 2002; Kouznetsova et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: SYCP3 has a role in chromosome compaction and stabilisation of the cohesin core.
source: These findings suggest a role for SYCP3 in chromosome compaction and stabilisation of the cohesin core.
evidence: Inferred from the structural consequences of SYCP3 deficiency.

claim: Ectopic expression of SYCP3 in somatic cells leads to the formation of fibre-like higher order assemblies with a regular repeating pattern of approximately 20 nm periodicity.
source: The ectopic expression of SYCP3 in somatic cells leads to the formation of fibre-like higher order assemblies that show a regular repeating pattern with a periodicity of approximately 20 nm (Yuan et al., 1998; Baier et al., 2007a, 2007b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Assembly of SYCP3 fibres is dependent on the presence of the last six amino acids of SYCP3.
source: Their assembly is dependent on the presence of the last six amino acids of SYCP3, which have been well conserved throughout evolution (Baier et al., 2007b; Fraune et al., 2012a).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Several SYCP3 mutations have been identified in infertile men and women with a history of recurrent pregnancy loss.
source: At the clinical level, several SYCP3 mutations have been identified in infertile men and women with a history of recurrent pregnancy loss (Miyamoto et al., 2003; Bolor et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: SYCP3 is ectopically expressed in a variety of primary tumours, which is associated with an increased rate of aneuploidy.
source: Furthermore, SYCP3 is ectopically expressed in a variety of primary tumours, which is associated with an increased rate of aneuploidy caused by inhibition of double-strand break DNA repair through homologous recombination by BRCA2 and RAD51 (Hosoya et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claim: SYCP3Core (amino acids 66-230) is highly stable and can be purified in large quantities to near homogeneity.
source: We thus identified a core region of human SYCP3, corresponding to amino acids 66–230 (SYCP3Core), that is highly stable and can be purified in large quantities to near homogeneity.
evidence: Supported by experimental purification data.

claim: SYCP3Core has an α-helical content of 93% (155 amino acids).
source: Circular dichroism analysis showed an α-helical content of 93% (155 amino acids) and 66% (180 amino acids) for SYCP3Core and SYCP3FL respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by circular dichroism spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SYCP3FL has an α-helical content of 66% (180 amino acids).
source: Circular dichroism analysis showed an α-helical content of 93% (155 amino acids) and 66% (180 amino acids) for SYCP3Core and SYCP3FL respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by circular dichroism spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both SYCP3Core and SYCP3FL demonstrate co-operative unfolding during thermal denaturation with a melting temperature of approximately 65°C.
source: both proteins demonstrated co-operative unfolding during thermal denaturation with a melting temperature of approximately 65°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by CD temperature melt data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: SYCP3Core eluted in a single peak with molecular weight 78.6 kDa, closely matching its theoretical tetramer size of 79.5 kDa.
source: SYCP3Core and SYCP3FL eluted in single peaks of molecular weights 78.6 and 110 kDa respectively (Figure 2A,B), closely matching their theoretical tetramer sizes of 79.5 and 111 kDa.
evidence: Supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SYCP3FL eluted in a single peak with molecular weight 110 kDa, closely matching its theoretical tetramer size of 111 kDa.
source: SYCP3Core and SYCP3FL eluted in single peaks of molecular weights 78.6 and 110 kDa respectively (Figure 2A,B), closely matching their theoretical tetramer sizes of 79.5 and 111 kDa.
evidence: Supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The tetrameric status of SYCP3Core was confirmed by analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC), which indicated a highly asymmetric structure with an estimated frictional ratio (f/f0) of 2.1.
source: The tetrameric status of SYCP3Core was confirmed by analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC), which further indicated a highly asymmetric structure with an estimated frictional ratio (f/f0) of 2.1 (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by AUC experimental data.

claim: Amino acids 66–230 of human SYCP3 form a core helical structure that mediates its assembly in a constitutive tetramer.
source: Together, these findings demonstrate that amino acids 66–230 of human SYCP3 form a core helical structure that mediates its assembly in a constitutive tetramer.
evidence: Inferred from CD, SEC-MALS, and AUC data.

claim: The X-ray crystal structure of SYCP3Core was solved at a resolution of 2.4 Å exploiting the single-wavelength anomalous diffraction of crystals soaked in sodium iodide.
source: The X-ray crystal structure of SYCP3Core was solved at a resolution of 2.4 Å exploiting the single-wavelength anomalous diffraction of crystals soaked in sodium iodide; the SYCP3Core structure was refined against native data at 2.2 Å (Table 1; Figure 2—figure supplements 2, 3).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data collection and refinement statistics in Table 1.

claim: The SYCP3Core structure was refined against native data at 2.2 Å.
source: The X-ray crystal structure of SYCP3Core was solved at a resolution of 2.4 Å exploiting the single-wavelength anomalous diffraction of crystals soaked in sodium iodide; the SYCP3Core structure was refined against native data at 2.2 Å (Table 1; Figure 2—figure supplements 2, 3).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data collection and refinement statistics in Table 1.

claim: The overall architecture of SYCP3 is an extended rod-like structure that spans approximately 20 nm in length.
source: The overall architecture of SYCP3 is an extended rod-like structure that spans approximately 20 nm in length (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The helical chains of the SYCP3 tetramer are arranged in an alternating anti-parallel fashion, such that each end of the tetramer contains two N-termini and two C-termini.
source: The helical chains of the SYCP3 tetramer are arranged in an alternating anti-parallel fashion, such that each end of the tetramer contains two N-termini and two C-termini.
evidence: Supported by the crystal structure.

claim: The SYCP3 structure undergoes a left-handed 90° rotation along its length so that the two N-termini at each end of the tetramer lie in orthogonal planes.
source: The SYCP3 structure undergoes a left-handed 90° rotation along its length so that the two N-termini at each end of the tetramer lie in orthogonal planes.
evidence: Supported by the crystal structure.

claim: The tetrameric assembly is constructed from a combination of four-helix bundles and coiled-coil motifs.
source: The tetrameric assembly is constructed from a combination of four-helix bundles and coiled-coil motifs.
evidence: Supported by the crystal structure.

claim: Each of the four SYCP3 chains adopts a unique conformation.
source: A noticeable consequence of this asymmetrical assembly is that each of the four SYCP3 chains adopts a unique conformation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each four-helix bundle contains a bipartite hydrophobic core consisting of a cluster of aromatic residues proximal to the middle of the tetramer and a more distal region centred around tryptophan W111.
source: Each bundle contains a bipartite hydrophobic core consisting of a cluster of aromatic residues proximal to the middle of the tetramer and a more distal region centred around tryptophan W111 (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: W111 adopts two distinct conformations in chains A and C.
source: Interestingly, W111 adopts two distinct conformations in chains A and C (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2): in both cases, the indole ring packs against L197B/D, but engages in alternative hydrogen bonding with Q201B (W111A) or D194D (W111C).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The centre of the SYCP3 tetramer is intrinsically asymmetrical as parallel chains B and D interact in a coiled-coil, keeping chains A and C apart by steric exclusion.
source: The centre of the SYCP3 tetramer is intrinsically asymmetrical as parallel chains B and D interact in a coiled-coil, keeping chains A and C apart by steric exclusion.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis.

claim: The central region likely oscillates between two conformations, in which the coiled-coil encompasses either chains B and D or chains A and C.
source: Instead, the central region likely oscillates between two conformations, in which the coiled-coil encompasses either chains B and D or chains A and C.
evidence: Inferred from the symmetry of the four identical chains and structural constraints.

claim: This dynamic interchange would allow torsional rotation around the longitudinal axis of SYCP3.
source: This dynamic interchange is supported by the abundance of conserved glutamine residues and would allow torsional rotation around the longitudinal axis of SYCP3.
evidence: Inferred from structural features and conservation patterns.

claim: The higher crystallographic B-factors of the backbone atoms in the central region relative to rest of the structure support a dynamic rather than fixed conformation.
source: Nevertheless, the higher crystallographic B-factors of the backbone atoms in the central region relative to rest of the structure support a dynamic rather than fixed conformation (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by B-factor analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: SYCP3ΔCt6 (amino acids 1–230) shows double-stranded DNA-binding, with the formation of a discrete protein-DNA complex at a Kd of 0.20 μM.
source: Analysis by electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) and fluorescence anisotropy using SYCP3ΔCt6 (amino acids 1–230) showed double-stranded DNA-binding, with the formation of a discrete protein-DNA complex at a Kd of 0.20 μM (Figure 4B,H).
evidence: Supported by EMSA and fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 4B,H.

claim: DNA-binding by SYCP3 was dependent on the N-terminal regions, as it was not detected for SYCP3Core.
source: DNA-binding was dependent on the N-terminal regions of SYCP3, as it was not detected for SYCP3Core (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The N-termini of SYCP3 contain two conserved basic patches, BP1 (52-KRRKKR-57) and BP2 (88-KRKR-91).
source: The N-termini of SYCP3 contain two conserved basic patches, BP1 (52-KRRKKR-57) and BP2 (88-KRKR-91) (Figure 4A)
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Alanine mutation of BP1 or BP2 in SYCP3ΔCt6 caused a substantial reduction in DNA binding affinity.
source: alanine mutation of BP1 or BP2 in SYCP3ΔCt6 (ΔBP1 and ΔBP2, respectively) caused a substantial reduction in binding affinity (Figure 4D,E,H)
evidence: Supported by EMSA and fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 4D,E,H.

claim: Mutation of both BP1 and BP2 completely eliminated DNA-binding by SYCP3ΔCt6.
source: whilst mutation of both patches (ΔBP1+2) completely eliminated DNA-binding by SYCP3ΔCt6 (Figure 4F,H).
evidence: Supported by EMSA and fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 4F,H.

claim: For all SYCP3ΔCt6 basic patch mutants, the tetrameric structure was confirmed by SEC-MALS.
source: For all SYCP3ΔCt6 basic patch mutants, the tetrameric structure was confirmed by SEC-MALS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The antiparallel arrangement of chains in the SYCP3 tetramer predicts that SYCP3 can interact simultaneously with two DNA molecules, one at either end of the tetramer.
source: The antiparallel arrangement of chains in the SYCP3 tetramer predicts that SYCP3 can interact simultaneously with two DNA molecules, one at either end of the tetramer (Figure 4I).
evidence: Inferred from the structural arrangement and DNA-binding data.

claim: Full length SYCP3 readily self-assembles into filamentous structures or fibres of 50–200 nm width, and up to 5 μm in length.
source: Analysis by electron microscopy revealed that full length SYCP3 readily self-assembles into filamentous structures or fibres of 50–200 nm width, and up to 5 μm in length (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The SYCP3 fibres display a regular pattern of alternate light and dark striations, with a repeating unit of approximately 23 nm.
source: The SYCP3 fibres display a regular pattern of alternate light and dark striations, with a repeating unit of approximately 23 nm.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy observations.

claim: The striated appearance of SYCP3 fibres closely resembles the ultrastructures formed upon heterologous expression of SYCP3 in vivo.
source: The striated appearance closely resembles the ultrastructures formed upon heterologous expression of SYCP3 in vivo (Yuan et al., 1998) and the SC lateral element in a number of species (Westergaard and von Wettstein, 1972).
evidence: Supported by comparison to published studies.

claim: Fibre formation is eliminated by removal of the last six amino acids of the protein (SYCP3ΔCt6).
source: Fibre formation is eliminated by removal of the last six amino acids of the protein (SYCP3ΔCt6), in agreement with a previous report (Baier et al., 2007a)
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data and citation to previous study.

claim: Fibre formation is eliminated by alanine mutation of a short stretch of conserved amino acids, 69-EVQNML-74 (SYCP3ΔNt6) N-terminal to the SYCP3 core.
source: or by alanine mutation of a short stretch of conserved amino acids, 69-EVQNML-74 (SYCP3ΔNt6) N-terminal to the SYCP3 core (Figures 4A, 5C,D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figures 5C,D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Self-assembly of SYCP3 is mediated by specific amino acid motifs in the N- and C-terminal tails of the tetrameric core structure.
source: Therefore, self-assembly of SYCP3 is mediated by specific amino acid motifs in the N- and C-terminal tails of the tetrameric core structure.
evidence: Inferred from the effects of deleting or mutating N- and C-terminal sequences on fibre formation.

claim: The presence of DNA is compatible with higher order assembly of SYCP3 in vitro.
source: The presence of self-association and DNA-binding motifs within tetrameric ends suggests that both processes must be closely integrated; accordingly, we find that the presence of DNA is compatible with higher order assembly in vitro (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: SYCP3 may impose the long-distance organisation of the chromosome axis by self-assembly in a three-dimensional lattice in which chromosomal DNA is looped between the 20 nm physical struts provided by each tetramer.
source: Thus, SYCP3 may impose the long-distance organisation of the chromosome axis by self-assembly in a three-dimensional lattice in which chromosomal DNA is looped between the 20 nm physical struts provided by each tetramer (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Torsional rotation of SYCP3 may be critical in relieving strains in the DNA backbone that build during recombination and crossover formation.
source: Acting as a molecular spacer, torsional rotation of SYCP3 may be critical in relieving strains in the DNA backbone that build during recombination and crossover formation.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the structural features of SYCP3.

claim: The model provides a molecular basis for the known increase in chromosome axis length in oocytes of SYCP3-deficient mice.
source: The model provides a molecular basis for the known increase in chromosome axis length in oocytes of SYCP3-deficient mice (Yuan et al., 2002).
evidence: The model is used to explain previously published observations.

claim: The model predicts the formation of one chromatin loop for every two repeating units in the SYCP3 fibre (46 nm), closely matching the known evolutionarily conserved loop density of ∼20 per 1 μm of chromosome axis.
source: It further predicts the formation of one chromatin loop for every two repeating units in the SYCP3 fibre (46 nm), closely matching the known evolutionarily conserved loop density of ∼20 per 1 μm of chromosome axis (Kleckner, 2006).
evidence: The model prediction is compared to known data from the literature.

claim: SC assembly depends upon the regular and compact meiotic chromosome architecture imposed by SYCP3.
source: We envisage that SC assembly depends upon the regular and compact meiotic chromosome architecture imposed by SYCP3, explaining the formation of only short fragmented SC structures upon SYCP3 deficiency in mice (Yuan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on the model and published observations.

claim: All SYCP3 mutations reported in human male infertility and female recurrent pregnancy loss affect the C-terminal sequence of the protein.
source: Furthermore, all SYCP3 mutations reported in human male infertility and female recurrent pregnancy loss affect the C-terminal sequence of the protein (Miyamoto et al., 2003; Bolor et al., 2009; Nishiyama et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: SYCP3 mutations affecting the C-terminal sequence would block higher order assembly whilst retaining tetramer formation.
source: our structural analysis shows that these mutations would block higher order assembly whilst retaining tetramer formation, confirming a key role for meiotic chromosome organisation by SYCP3 in human fertility.
evidence: Inferred from the structural analysis and mutation data.

claim: EM studies of the mammalian SC have revealed that the lateral element is comprised of two parallel filaments.
source: EM studies of the mammalian SC have revealed that the lateral element is comprised of two parallel filaments (Comings and Okada, 1971; Dietrich et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to published EM studies.

claim: SYCP3 may compact chromosomal DNA into two parallel assemblies within the lateral element, separating sister chromatid DNA locally in the midline whilst retaining cohesion in the chromatin loops.
source: It is interesting to speculate that, instead of a single higher order structure, SYCP3 may compact chromosomal DNA into two parallel assemblies within the lateral element, separating sister chromatid DNA locally in the midline whilst retaining cohesion in the chromatin loops.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on EM observations and the model.

claim: The structural organisation of sister chromatid DNA by SYCP3 may inhibit inter-sister recombination whilst permitting inter-homologue recombination.
source: In such a model, the structural organisation of sister chromatid DNA may inhibit inter-sister recombination whilst permitting inter-homologue recombination.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the model.

claim: In vivo, SYCP3 recruitment to the chromosome axis is abrogated upon disruption of SYCP2, STAG3 or REC8/RAD21L.
source: In vivo, SYCP3 function depends upon SYCP2 and the meiotic cohesin core, as SYCP3 recruitment to the chromosome axis is abrogated upon disruption of SYCP2, STAG3 or REC8/RAD21L (Yang et al., 2006; Llano et al., 2012; Fukuda et al., 2014; Winters et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: SYCP3 loading on the chromosome axis must be tightly regulated to prevent formation of unproductive cytoplasmic structures.
source: The intrinsic propensity of SYCP3 to self-assemble into higher-order structures in vitro and in vivo (Yuan et al., 1998) suggests that its loading on the chromosome axis must be tightly regulated to prevent formation of unproductive cytoplasmic structures.
evidence: Inferred from the self-assembly properties and cited observations.

claim: Protein mediators, possibly SYCP2, may bind to SYCP3 and prevent its self-assembly until delivery onto chromosomal DNA.
source: This may be achieved by protein mediators, possibly SYCP2, that bind to SYCP3 and prevent its self-assembly until delivery onto chromosomal DNA.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the need for regulation.

claim: A role for meiotic cohesins in determining loop length is hinted at by the known shortening of the SYCP3-bound chromosome axis length upon disruption of SMC1β or REC8.
source: A role for meiotic cohesins is hinted at by the known shortening of the SYCP3-bound chromosome axis length upon disruption of SMC1β or REC8 (Bannister et al., 2004; Revenkova et al., 2004; Novak et al., 2008).
evidence: Inferred from published observations cited.

claim: Some SYCP3 is retained on chromosome arms until metaphase.
source: Completion of recombination and crossover formation is accompanied by dissolution of the SC structure and SYCP3 removal, although some SYCP3 is retained on chromosome arms until metaphase (Parra et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans crossover sites are associated with a local 0.4–0.5 µm elongation in chromosome axis length.
source: The recent observation that in Caenorhabditis elegans crossover sites are associated with a local 0.4–0.5 µm elongation in chromosome axis length (Libuda et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claim: SYCP3 disassembly may be regulated locally to yield a looser chromatin structure at points of established crossovers.
source: suggests the intriguing possibility that SYCP3 disassembly may be regulated locally to yield a looser chromatin structure at points of established crossovers.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the cited observation.

claim: The work has yielded the first atomic view of an SC protein, the lateral element component SYCP3.
source: The work described here has yielded the first atomic view of an SC protein, the lateral element component SYCP3
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the crystal structure.

claim: The work has provided a molecular basis for SYCP3 function in the compaction and organisation of the meiotic chromosome.
source: and has provided a molecular basis for SYCP3 function in the compaction and organisation of the meiotic chromosome.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: The tetramer provides a length of 20 nm between the extremes of its C-terminal coiled-coils.
source: The tetramer provides a length of 20 nm between the extremes of its C-terminal coiled-coils (measured at 196.1 and 199.9 Å between Gln220 Cα atoms of chains A and B, and chains C and D, respectively).
evidence: Supported by measurements from the crystal structure.

claim: The majority of secondary structure, and the overall stability of the protein, emanate from the 66–230 core region.
source: Thus, the majority of secondary structure, and the overall stability of the protein, emanate from the 66–230 core region.
evidence: Inferred from CD and thermal denaturation data comparing SYCP3Core and SYCP3FL.

claim: The high-salt dependency of full length SYCP3 could be eliminated by removing six amino acids from the C-terminal end of the protein.
source: We found that the high-salt dependency could be eliminated by removing six amino acids from the C-terminal end of the protein that are known to be essential for fibre formation upon heterologous expression (Baier et al., 2007a).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and citation.

claim: Unwanted proteolysis of the recombinant sample was alleviated by removing the N-terminal 65 amino acids that are predicted to be largely unstructured.
source: Unwanted proteolysis of the recombinant sample was alleviated by removing the N-terminal 65 amino acids that are predicted to be largely unstructured (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations.

claim: The crystals contain two tetramers in the asymmetric unit.
source: The crystals contain two tetramers in the asymmetric unit; the tetramers are almost identical both between and within iodide derivative and native structures (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The extensive network of hydrophobic and polar interactions within the two helical bundles is likely to be responsible for the high thermal stability of the SYCP3 structure.
source: The extensive network of hydrophobic and polar interactions within the two helical bundles is likely to be responsible for the high thermal stability of the SYCP3 structure.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis and thermal stability data.

claim: The proximal aromatic-rich core of the four-helix bundle results from the close packing of Y125A/C, F129A/C and F133A/C with Y179B/D and F182B/D.
source: The proximal aromatic-rich core of the four-helix bundle results from the close packing of Y125A/C, F129A/C and F133A/C with Y179B/D and F182B/D
evidence: Supported by structural analysis.

claim: The two hydrophobic cores of the four-helix bundle are separated by a solvent-rich layer of polar residues, featuring at its centre R118A/C, bonded via salt link with E190B/D.
source: The two hydrophobic cores of the four-helix bundle are separated by a solvent-rich layer of polar residues, featuring at its centre R118A/C, bonded via salt link with E190B/D.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis.

claim: At its distal end, the four-helix bundle morphs into a parallel coiled-coil between the C-termini of chains B and D, flanked by the N-terminal helical segments of chains A and C that splay apart.
source: At its distal end, the four-helix bundle morphs into a parallel coiled-coil between the C-termini of chains B and D, flanked by the N-terminal helical segments of chains A and C that splay apart (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The coiled-coil is held together by a heptad containing I150B/D, F154B/D, Q157B/D and L161B/D at the interface.
source: The coiled-coil is held together by a heptad containing I150B/D, F154B/D, Q157B/D and L161B/D at the interface
evidence: Supported by structural analysis.

claim: A hydrogen bonding network between highly-conserved glutamine residues Q157B/D and Q158B/D interrupts the continuity of the hydrophobic interactions at the heart of the coiled-coil.
source: A hydrogen bonding network between highly-conserved glutamine residues Q157B/D and Q158B/D interrupts the continuity of the hydrophobic interactions at the heart of the coiled-coil
evidence: Supported by structural analysis.

claim: The boundaries of the central coiled-coil are marked by tryptophan residues W136A/C and W136B/D, which define points of conformational transition to a four-helix bundle in the two arms of the tetramer.
source: The boundaries of the central coiled-coil are marked by tryptophan residues W136A/C and W136B/D, which define points of conformational transition to a four-helix bundle in the two arms of the tetramer (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: In both conformations, the left-handed 90° rotation would be retained; interchange between conformations would require a transitory super-helical unwinding of the central region.
source: In both conformations, the left-handed 90° rotation would be retained; interchange between conformations would require a transitory super-helical unwinding of the central region.
evidence: Inferred from structural constraints.

claim: In the crystal structure, torsional rotation is precluded by the crystal lattice, freezing the central coiled-coil in a single conformation.
source: In the crystal structure, torsional rotation is precluded by the crystal lattice, freezing the central coiled-coil in a single conformation.
evidence: Inferred from crystallographic constraints.

claim: GST-SYCP3BP1+2 (amino acids 49–93) binds DNA with significantly lower affinity than SYCP3ΔCt6.
source: We further detected DNA binding by a GST fusion protein containing amino acids 49–93 (GST-SYCP3BP1+2) spanning both basic patches; its significantly lower affinity than that of SYCP3ΔCt6 (Figure 4G) indicates that the tetrameric architecture may be important to orientate correctly the DNA-binding regions of the protein.
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The tetrameric architecture may be important to orientate correctly the DNA-binding regions of the protein.
source: its significantly lower affinity than that of SYCP3ΔCt6 (Figure 4G) indicates that the tetrameric architecture may be important to orientate correctly the DNA-binding regions of the protein.
evidence: Inferred from the difference in DNA-binding affinity between GST-SYCP3BP1+2 and SYCP3ΔCt6.

claim: The difference in DNA-binding affinity between ΔBP1 and SYCP3Core suggests that additional amino acids surrounding the basic patch residues contribute to DNA binding.
source: The difference in DNA-binding affinity between ΔBP1 and SYCP3Core, which includes BP2 but not BP1, suggests that additional amino acids surrounding the basic patch residues contribute to DNA binding (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of DNA-binding data for different constructs.

claim: The comparable size of the repeating unit relative to the length of the SYCP3Core structure suggests that the fibre contains stacked layers of SYCP3 molecules brought into parallel alignment by self-associating interactions.
source: The comparable size of the repeating unit relative to the length of the SYCP3Core structure suggests that the fibre contains stacked layers of SYCP3 molecules brought into parallel alignment by self-associating interactions (Figure 5B).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of EM periodicity and crystal structure length.

claim: The proposed packing of SYCP3 molecules within the fibre would bring into juxtaposition the N- and C-terminal tails originating from tetramers located in adjacent layers.
source: The proposed packing of SYCP3 molecules within the fibre would bring into juxtaposition the N- and C-terminal tails originating from tetramers located in adjacent layers.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model for fibre assembly.

claim: Self-assembly may be driven by co-operative interactions of the terminal regions of the SYCP3 tetramers, extending recursively across the width of the fibre.
source: Thus, self-assembly may be driven by co-operative interactions of the terminal regions of the SYCP3 tetramers, extending recursively across the width of the fibre (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model for fibre assembly.

claim: Such an arrangement of SYCP3 molecules would explain the regular striation pattern of the fibre, with layers of dense protein packing at the interface and looser, conformationally dynamic regions in the centre of the molecule accounting for the alternating dark and light bands.
source: Such an arrangement of SYCP3 molecules would explain the regular striation pattern of the fibre, with layers of dense protein packing at the interface and looser, conformationally dynamic regions in the centre of the molecule accounting for the alternating dark and light bands.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the proposed model.

claim: The presence of self-association and DNA-binding motifs within tetrameric ends suggests that both processes must be closely integrated.
source: The presence of self-association and DNA-binding motifs within tetrameric ends suggests that both processes must be closely integrated
evidence: Inferred from the structural organization of functional motifs.

claim: Co-operative loading of further SYCP3 molecules onto DNA would reinforce nascent loops, and then bridge between them through self-assembly interactions with SYCP3 molecules of adjacent loops.
source: Co-operative loading of further SYCP3 molecules onto DNA would reinforce nascent loops, and then bridge between them through self-assembly interactions with SYCP3 molecules of adjacent loops.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model for chromosome organization.

claim: Completion of the self-assembly process would eventually link all loops in one continuous structure extending for the length of the chromosome axis.
source: Completion of the self-assembly process would eventually link all loops in one continuous structure extending for the length of the chromosome axis.

claim: The resultant ultrastructure of the meiotic chromosome axis would contain discrete stretches of chromosomal DNA compacted in a concertina-like manner within the newly formed lateral element, interspersed with chromatin loops protruding from the SC.
source: The resultant ultrastructure of the meiotic chromosome axis would contain discrete stretches of chromosomal DNA compacted in a concertina-like manner within the newly formed lateral element, interspersed with chromatin loops protruding from the SC (Figure 6).
